edges.description: Loss of nuclear UNG removes the enzyme that excises AID-generated uracil from immunoglobulin switch-region DNA.
Reduced excision of switch-region uracil yields fewer abasic sites and the DNA nicks and double-strand breaks CSR requires.
Persistence of unexcised U:G lesions skews the point-mutation spectrum introduced during somatic hypermutation.
The precleavage block manifests as a measurable failure of in-vitro class-switch recombination in patient B cells.
Failure to switch constant regions prevents production of IgG, IgA and IgE and leaves IgM as the dominant isotype.
Cells that fail to complete class switching do not populate the switched-memory compartment.
B cells that cannot complete switching keep being driven by antigen, enlarging germinal centers and lymph nodes.
IgM is not converted to downstream isotypes and accumulates.
Failure to switch to Cgamma abolishes normal IgG production.
Failure to switch to Calpha abolishes normal IgA production.
Failure to switch to Cepsilon leaves IgE low or absent.
Without class switching, antigen-specific IgG responses to vaccines and neoantigens are poor.
Loss of switched IgG and secretory IgA removes opsonizing and mucosal antibody protection against encapsulated bacteria.

nodes.description: UNG deficiency does not abolish somatic hypermutation but distorts its spectrum. Unexcised U:G lesions persist and favour replication-associated G:C transitions, while the loss of abasic-site formation reduces G:C transversions. In the mouse this shows as a shift to ~95% transitions at G:C pairs; a single human UNG-deficient repertoire showed the same directional skew.

nodes.description: AID converts cytosine to uracil in single-stranded DNA at transcribed switch and variable regions. Without UNG, that uracil is not efficiently removed. The AID-directed step depends specifically on UNG being recruited to RPA-coated single-stranded DNA, a function separable from canonical repair of uracil in double-stranded genomic DNA. The unexcised U:G lesions propagate into the two downstream antibody-diversification failures.

nodes.description: Regular intravenous or subcutaneous IgG replacement is the mainstay, supplying the switched antibody patients cannot make and reducing infection frequency. It does not correct the underlying enzymatic defect.

The block is at a DNA precleavage step: without efficient uracil excision, switch regions are not cut, so recombination from Cmu to the downstream Cgamma, Calpha or Cepsilon constant regions fails. In human UNG deficiency this failure is profound, more severe than in the Ung-knockout mouse, where a mismatch-repair backup leaves switching only partly inhibited.

nodes.description: Homozygous Phe251Ser missense substitution in the UNG catalytic domain. The purified enzyme is active and stable in vitro, but in mammalian cells it is aberrantly sorted to mitochondria and degraded, so only ~0.4% of normal nuclear uracil-excision activity remains — explaining the hyper-IgM phenotype despite retained intrinsic catalytic capacity.

nodes.description: Uracil-DNA glycosylase is encoded by UNG, which produces a mitochondrial isoform (UNG1) and a nuclear isoform (UNG2); UNG2 is induced in activated germinal-center B cells. It hydrolyses the N-glycosidic bond of uracil in DNA, initiating base-excision repair by creating an abasic (AP) site. Biallelic UNG variants abolish or severely reduce this nuclear activity: truncating alleles yield catalytically dead protein, and the F251S missense allele produces an enzyme that is active in vitro but mistargeted to mitochondria and degraded in B cells, leaving only trace residual activity. This molecular lesion is the single upstream cause of the downstream class-switch and hypermutation defects.

nodes.description: Gene-targeted Ung-null mice reproduce the mechanism but not the full human severity: class-switch recombination is only partly inhibited (a mismatch-repair backup operates in mice), and somatic hypermutation at G:C pairs is shifted strongly toward transitions. Aged Ung-null mice develop B-cell lymphomas, a finding specific to the mouse that should not be read as a demonstrated human cancer risk.
